# Espresso Water Recipes

## Overview

Water is the largest single ingredient in a cup of coffee and the one I ignored for the longest time. I started with tap water, then filtered water, then a bottled brand that I liked, and only when a boiler came back from a repair with a furred element did I start to think about what was in the water rather than how it tasted. Plain distilled water is a poor brew water on its own, because it has no minerals to carry the coffee into solution and it tastes flat and hollow no matter how good the beans are. What I want is a small, known amount of hardness and a smaller, known amount of alkalinity, so the water extracts the coffee without dragging out the bitter and ashy notes. I mix my own from distilled water and a pair of dry salts, which sounds fussy but takes ten minutes a week. Once the minerals are under control the coffee tastes sweeter, the boiler stays cleaner, and I stop blaming the beans for faults that were never theirs. The whole recipe fits on an index card taped inside the cupboard door.

## Setup

I start from distilled or deionised water and add two salts by weight. Per litre I dissolve 1.2 g of magnesium sulphate and 0.5 g of potassium bicarbonate, which lands the mix at roughly 60 ppm hardness and 40 ppm alkalinity once the solution is uniform. I weigh the salts on the same scale I use for coffee, because a scoop is hopeless for this and the numbers drift with the grain size of the powder. The hardness gives the coffee something to cling to, and the alkalinity keeps the brew from turning sharp and sour, so both matter. My tap water carries chloride, and chloride is the one thing I will not tolerate, so I keep it below 5 ppm by using distilled as the base. I keep a TDS meter on the bench and check the mix against it rather than trusting the arithmetic alone. I make 5 L batches on a Sunday so I have enough for the week, and I store the bottles in a dark cupboard.

## Notes

The point of all this is that scale kills boilers, and the deposits come from the same minerals that make water taste good, so the trick is to keep them low enough to brew with and high enough to stop short of the metal. A magnesium hardness around 60 ppm is a sensible middle, and alkalinity near 40 ppm keeps the acidity of the roast in balance. I record the batch date on each bottle and use them oldest first, since the mix does not keep forever in an open bottle. I once chased a sour shot for a fortnight and it turned out to be the beans, not the water, which taught me to check the simple things first. I keep a small jar of each salt in the cupboard and a spare set of bottles, and the whole routine now takes less time than grinding a bag of coffee. If the coffee tastes chalky I know the alkalinity has drifted up, and if it tastes hollow the hardness has drifted down, so I adjust the next batch by a tenth of a gram and taste again. Three bottles of the mix sit in the cupboard at any time, which is enough for a full week of morning coffee.

## Troubleshooting

Chalky, flat coffee usually means too much alkalinity, so I drop the potassium bicarbonate a little in the next batch. Hollow, thin coffee points the other way, at too little hardness, and lifting the magnesium sulphate brings the body back. If the TDS meter reads high against my target, I check whether I have misread the scale or mixed a double batch before I pour anything out. A metallic or salty edge is chloride finding its way in, so I test the base water and the pipes and go back to distilled if I have to. If the machine starts to taste odd after a change of supply, the water is the first thing I look at rather than the last. I write the batch number on the bottle so I can trace a bad pot back to a single mix, which has saved me an afternoon of second guessing more than once. A full litre of the mix costs a few pence and covers three or four days of brewing. Two spare bottles live under the sink, and I fill them first so the older water is always used before the newer.
